This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews.

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Zubair Mohajir is one of Chicago’s most prolific new chefs and restaurateurs, behind such openings as Lilac Tiger, Mariela, Mirra, Sarima, and most recently, Muhājir, a restaurant that traces historical spice routes to tell the story of global migration. I talked to Mohajir about how the opening is going, how he thinks about collaboration across his different projects, and why Muhājir is finally the restaurant that feels like home.

Pre Shift: What did you want to explore with Muhājir that you hadn’t been able to do yet with your previous restaurants?

Zubair Mohajir: Muhājir is such a personal story for me, because my last name is Mohajir, and the meaning of “muhājir” in Arabic and Urdu is “one who migrates.” When the partition [of India and Pakistan] happened, the Muslims that were moved from India to Pakistan were named Muhājirs because they were migrated. In my family, we always wondered why that was our last name. When I started cooking [after working in finance], it really started to settle in. Our late maternal grandfather was obsessed with mapping where this family name came from. It comes from Southern Basra, Iraq, and that was so mind-blowing for me because it’s one of the biggest spice roads.

At Coach House for the past five years, I’ve been exploring ancient recipes in southern Spain and southern Portugal. [They] bring in pre-Crusade Muslim, Christian, Jewish [influences] that are also affected by the Southeast Asian traders coming on the spice road that shoots through the Mediterranean and hits North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula. I’m just obsessed with history and it started to become very evident for me that I really wanted to feed people, but with the context of where the food came from.

At Muhājir, it’s all about riding the spice road that runs from Portugal through the Mediterranean, through the Levantine [region], and then hits out of Basra, Iraq, into the Persian Gulf, and the first landmass it comes across is southern India, where I’m from. We’re all muhājirs — you know, all of our families came from somewhere, and that really has been the driving force for me.

Why did you decide to build the restaurant around live fire?

I’d never cooked on live fire, but we’re cooks, and it was going back to core things. I remember growing up in my grandmother’s house back home in India, and it’s not like there were gas stoves everywhere. When I decided that I was going to do Muhājir, it became so obvious to me that it couldn’t just be a sauté pan on a stove. The story that we wanted to tell had to be told through wood fire.

Is there a dish that feels especially representative of Muhājir?

We do a duck that is inspired by a 927-year-old recipe we found from southern Spain that is influenced by Roman garums, Muslim origins, and Jewish origins. We do this duck “experience,” where we take a whole duck, butcher it, and have the crown dry-aging for seven days. We take the wings and make a jus [and] take the legs and make a confit. We blast that duck crown over the fire when we start service every day, and then it gets finished in the brasa. If you’re sitting in the restaurant, you can see the ducks hanging over the fire.

When we present it, we have this beautiful ornate Turkish platter. There’s black raspberry achaar, the duck jus in a saucier, the duck rice next to it, the duck skin cut in these beautiful medallions on top almost like duck chicharrón, and then we’re also presenting the duck breast itself that has a very crispy skin. The top of that duck breast is the spice mix from that exact recipe that’s more than 900 years old, with cumin, coriander, cardamom, toasted pine nuts, red wine vinegar, and fish sauce. It’s a story of cross-cultural collaboration.

You have a bar called Bobo behind the restaurant. How do the two spaces complement each other?

Bobo’s really inspired by Jacob Dela Cruz, who’s my partner here. We built Sarima together, and it became very important to me to highlight his upbringing and his background as well. He was one who said, “You should name the restaurant Muhājir.” His point was that we’re all immigrants. I was like, “That’s such a simple statement, but such a profound statement.” It was kind of vice versa when we were talking about the bar: Jacob’s father is an amazing person and his name is Bho, and “bobo” in Tagalog means “silly” or “stupid,” as a term of endearment. We always say that as Spice Road-driven and transformative the food experience at Muhājir is, we still like to have fun.

If people are early for their reservation, we take them back to Bobo, or they stop by after dinner. You can’t get to Bobo without walking through the restaurant, so the spaces contribute to each other. If you came to Bobo, you might be like, “I want to eat there.” And if you come straight to Muhājir and see people walking back constantly, you might be like, “What’s happening back there?”

What has it been like to run Muhājir so far?

I wouldn’t say it’s easier [than my other restaurants], but now I don’t freak out. I’ve created a methodical way of approaching issues or problems head-on and figuring it out as a group or with the people that support us. We don’t have investors who are private equity firms; our investors are our guests. When it comes to managing expectations and navigating obstacles, you get better with repetition.

I’m living a dream. Sometimes, when you’re building restaurants with others, you’re not necessarily in the kitchen. [At Mirra, I] was like, “I’m helping create and build this concept, but that’s [chef Rishi Kumar’s] kitchen to run.” Here, it’s the home that I’ve been yearning for and working toward my whole career. I plan to be old in this place. Things have been so crazy and wild and amazing, but slowly, every day, I sit more and more in that moment where I’m like, “This is home.”

This interview has been edited and condensed.

In her pristine Los Angeles kitchen, Nora Lum—the actor, comedian, and rapper better known as Awkwafina—is standing over a stove with two burners and losing the fight with both. Ramen boils on one; Spam violently sizzles over the other. Surveying the spectacle over FaceTime, her nonagenarian grandmother, Powah, cackles and tells her (lovingly) that it looks like shit.

This scene opens Lum’s new show, Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook.

“Food is so important to being Asian,” she announces to the camera. “You can’t talk about being Asian without food being the thread that pulls it all together.” But what if, like the 38-year-old Lum, you can’t even steam an egg?

Family history complicates the answer further. Raised in Forest Hills, NY, the actor has considerable Queens cred (after all, her Comedy Central show was called Awkwafina Is Nora From Queens), but she is also descended from local restaurant royalty.

In 1952 her great-grandfather Jimmy Lum opened the family’s Chinese restaurant in Flushing, one of the first in the neighborhood at the time. “If you lived in New York, not just Queens, at a certain era, almost 10 out of 10 times, you remember Lum’s,” she says. (When I ask some of the food-world old heads I know about it, they respond immediately with memories of the pupu platter, the lobster egg rolls, and the glitzy, neon-lit decor.)

“I’ll cook for a chef any day. With my family, I’ll order out.”

Nora Lum aka Awkwafina, at Bistro Na's in Los Angeles.Photograph by Pat Martin

Lum, who is half Korean, previously explored her mother’s roots on an episode of No Taste Like Home With Antoni Porowski, but she knows little firsthand about her father’s family restaurant, which closed before she was born. “When they talk about it, it’s like they’re talking about a long-lost family member,” she says.

The Apple TV docuseries follows Lum as she meets and cooks with Asian American chefs and restaurateurs. Many of them are like her, restaurant kids who left and eventually found their way back on their own terms. “A lot of their families did not want them to go into the industry. They’re subverting the stereotype in a way,” she says of chefs like Cory Ng and Zhan Chen of NYC's Potluck Club, who help her resurrect Lum’s as a one-night pop-up.

“I always dreamed of being the intrepid restaurant worker,” Lum says. But her family’s attitude toward cooking was less romantic. “Whether it was dishes or cooking, no one trusted me with it. I convinced myself that I’m just not a cook.”

Zigzagging the country changed that, from blowing up a duck at Mister Jiu’s in San Francisco to manning the wok at the Culinary Institute of America in New York to touring Texas barbecue joints with her friend and fellow comedian Jimmy O. Yang. They stopped by Curry Boys BBQ in San Antonio, where traditional Texas brisket is served atop a bowl of green Thai curry, followed by Eaker Barbecue in Fredericksburg for bulgogi sausage. “Seeing Asian people in this environment that’s so Texas, where the two cultures are very different,” broadened her perception of how chefs layer their influences in a way that wasn’t a compromise.

The pleasure of the show is watching Lum encounter new experiences. At a whole-hog barbecue in a Hawaii-set episode, chef Mark Noguchi tells her they’re going to use an imu, an underground pit oven. She lights up, not missing a beat. “Like the bird?”

Her ignorance is played for laughs but is also the source of the show’s unusual tenderness. Lum is game for almost anything, even when she has no idea what is happening. “It’s like one of those school nightmares where you hadn’t completed the class and then you’re just walking in for the test,” she says.

Things go wrong, and Lum is put through the wringer. The show doesn’t spare her discomfort, but what surprised her most was how gentle cooking for chefs turned out to be. “I’ll cook for a chef any day,” she says. “With my family, I’ll order out.”

Lately she’s perfecting her Bolognese and careful not to oversell the show’s resolution. “As much as it was a journey of food and collective Asian culture, it was also self-discovery,” she says, catching herself. “Probably in a narcissistic way—there’s still a question mark as to what it all means.”

Welcome to the Eater Cocktail Heatmap, focusing on the hottest new bar openings in New York every month.

Eater editors do thorough reporting on the most exciting restaurant openings to hit the city, as well as smaller openings worth having on the radar. In this monthly map, we narrow the field to cocktail bars that are drawing the most excitement, buzz, crowds, and early positive chatter, focusing on spots that have only been open for six months or less. When an Eater editor has already been to a place, we share insider tips on what to expect and what’s worth ordering as well.

New to the list in October: We’ve added Japanese cocktail bar Don’t Be Shy in Hudson Square; massive Chinese-leaning cocktail bar/restaurant/karaoke lounge Rewind in Long Island City; South Asian speakeasy Jam & Jaggery in the East Village; and retro bars FKA in the East Village and Velvet Cowboy on the Upper West Side. For now, we’ve removed Bar Chimera, Peek Inn, and Hidden Rivers Beer Garden.

For related drinking guides, check out Eater NY’s picks for the best cocktail bars, dive bars, and wine bars. And for more New York dining recommendations, check out the new hotspots in Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens. In need of an insider’s perspective on how to eat well, no matter where you are in NYC? Pick up our book: The Eater Guide to New York City.

The Jacob’s Pickles team turned its space on the Upper West Side (which relocated to Columbus Avenue) into Velvet Cowboy, a new 1970s Southwestern cocktail bar, in September. Find $5 bar snacks, like a take on the McRib sandwich, chili-cheese fries, and a huge funnel cake hanging from a stand.

A massive new restaurant-cocktail bar-karaoke lounge, Rewind, opened in Long Island City this September and is co-founded with AYS Hospitality, which runs Mr. Moto’s restaurant portfolio. The drinks menu, developed by beverage director Ken Chen, who had been at Taipei gastropub Indulge Experimental Bistro, took cues from tea, the Chinese zodiac, and the five elements. Tipsy Blossom represents fire signs and bitter elements, made with whisky, shochu, chrysanthemum, pear, hawthorn, licorice root, and goji berry. The food menu includes truffle-mushroom congee, Taiwanese fried chicken, and wagyu donburi. Per the name, people enter the space by pressing a “rewind” button on a retro boombox outside.

The team behind West Village cocktail lounge Dandelion expanded with Keepers, a new neighborhood-leaning bar and pizzeria, in July. Drinks, courtesy of Ricky Dolinsky (formerly of the View), include interesting Negronis such as the Black Forest, a drinkable homage to Ben & Jerry’s Cherry Garcia; spritzes; and frozens. Food-wise, find crispy tavern pies.

Bernie and Herb’s comes from a trio of 169 Bar alums who wanted to do a neighborhood spot that’s affordable and stays open until late. The bar opened in July, housed in the space that had been part of Coffee Shop, the Brazilian late-night icon in the area for 30 years. Look for drinks around $10 and inexpensive bar food like hot dogs, pulled pork sandwiches, and more.

FKA, which stands for “Formerly Known As,” is all about retro vibes since it opened in September in the East Village. Look for dollar East Coast oysters; dishes like lamb tartare, pimento cheese, Frito pies, and cheeseburgers; activities like pinball and Big Buck Hunter; and drinks like strawberry daiquiris, natural wines, and $8 beer-and-shot combos.

Chef Aarthi Sampath debuted a new speakeasy underneath her East Village restaurant Drāvida in September. Jam & Jaggery takes on the same South Asian foundation, with drinks like the Dirty Currytini with olive vermouth and curry leaves, and the Gola Chaat with shochu, yogurt, pomegranate, tamarind, herbs, and aloo bhujia, the latter of which is a spiced boiled potato snack. Sampath is offering some of her upstairs snacks, along with an Indian-ish burger.

The team, whose bar history includes Bar Valentina and Employees Only, took over the former Bandits space with a French-leaning bar. Bar Etienne opened in the West Village in August, with a very banana-y rum cocktail along with tomato martinis, chocolate Negronis, and wines. The bistro food menu includes steak au poivre and French onion-grilled cheeses, plus desserts created in collaboration with nearby Claude Bakery, such as tarte tatin and that chocolate cake.

New Hudson Square cocktail bar Don’t Be Shy is meant to evoke Tokyo’s stylish Ginza district since it opened in September. Head bartender Shinya Yamao, who worked at now-closed Piora and Tribeca sake bar Shigure, developed a Japanese cocktail menu with a special Trip to Japan menu available only at the nine-seat bar counter, exploring Japanese history and regionality, like the Edo, made with a potato-miso-flavored vodka and a sweet potato-Campari ice cube. Other drinks are available at the table seats, such as the Miyajima, which has momo nigori sake, red shiso, and lemon. Food includes wagyu and egg salad sandos and umami burrata with taro chips, pecans, dashi, and tomato sorbet.

Alas, Enid’s isn’t coming back, but the Greenpoint Fish & Lobster team turned its Greenpoint address into a new bar paying tribute to another shuttered neighborhood fixture. They opened Matches (a nod to Bar Matchless) in August, with $16 cocktails, along with burgers and steak frites.

Co-owners and couple Mercury Tin and Philip Dizard opened Tin’s on the Lower East Side as their ode to their life experiences. It’s a two-floor, New York-meets-Shanghai bar and restaurant that opened in July (and thankfully, the kitchen is fully open, serving those Shanghai-style dumplings). Drinks pay homage to those blending influences; see: an ode to the Dead Rabbit’s Irish coffee with a Shanghai dirty coffee twist.

A new cocktail bar devoted to all things rum opened in Williamsburg in April in the former original Gertie space. Echo Lake offers $12 daily daiquiris and a lager/rum shot combo cutely called Tiny and a Tot, plus seafood-centric plates like oysters with tepache mignonette and green coconut curry chowder. The new bar comes from beverage power couple Chloe Frechette (the former executive editor at Eater sibling site Punch) and Paul McGee, who cut his teeth at Chicago’s now-closed tropical bar Lost Lake. The duo is also featuring their own collection of liquid loot within the intimate basement rum bar, Undercurrent.

The team behind Mexican fine-dining restaurant Corima and burrito hot spot Vato opened a new bar in downtown Manhattan this April. Bar Chucho, a comparatively casual bar counterpart to Corima, offers fantastic drinks like the Desert Rain with sotol, along with lots of micheladas and familiar food like the carne asada-esque burger.

New Williamsburg bar Dokidoki, which opened in July, is just a fun meshing of Latin and Japanese cultures, courtesy of co-owners and cocktail vets A-K Hada, an alum of Please Don’t Tell and Existing Conditions; and Christian Suzuki-Orellana, a semifinalist on Netflix’s Drink Masters. With just a beer and wine license, they’re whipping up fun martinis and honeydew “margaritas” made with shochu, sakes, and local meads. The Japanese-Puerto Rican-Salvadoran bar snacks include a katsu sandwich made with cod on shokupan bread. It’s a small yet cozy space.

Brooklyn cocktail bar Grand Army alums Patty Dennison and Ally Marrone opened their own bar in Williamsburg in May, taking over what was the Ensenada space. The press release describes Kinda Nice as a mix of “late-night diner culture” and “dive bar spontaneity,” which translates to savory and sweet cocktails like the guava Negroni with malted milk and pisco; the Greek Salad martini with Tomato Crop vodka and a piparra brine; and a tequila drink with lime sherbet and a choice of blueberry or strawberry amaro and tequila. The duo also debuted their downstairs dive bar at the address, Shenanigans, with beers, highballs, boilermakers, and DJs (dancing is encouraged)

New Bushwick bar the Museum Bar + Gift Shop is meant to feel like a hella fun natural history museum, which opened in June. The space is covered in illuminated fossils, crystals, and dinosaur heads. The drinks list continues that thread, with the Insectarium, a Negroni-ish drink with insects; and the Ocean Life made with rum, coconut, limes, Curaçao, and cuttlefish ink. items.title: Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life
items.author: Matthew Kepnes
items.summary: Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning
items.text:
Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.


Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.


I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.


Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.


In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

Day 1: Immersion in the Art Walk


This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.


The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.


Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.


After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.


After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.


Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.


In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.


Day 2: The Grandeur of the Historic Center


The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.


For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.


After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.


For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.


As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.


For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.


Day 4: UNESCO World Heritage Wonders


Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.


One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.


Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).


Day 5: Off-the-Beaten-Path Treasures


On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.


The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).


To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.


***


While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

全球债券收益率攀升至数十年高位，但经济与市场迄今展现出异乎寻常的韧性。随着欧洲主权债券市场等领域压力初现，这一韧性能否持续，成为市场最迫切的追问。


高盛最新研究报告汇集了国际货币基金组织、穆迪分析及高盛经济学家的多方研判。IMF顾问Tobias Adrian持审慎乐观立场，认为只要收益率上行不失序加速，全球经济有望延续抗压态势；高盛经济学家则预计高利率对美国经济增长的拖累将相对温和，2027年约为0.2个百分点，但若收益率持续维持当前水平，拖累效应将扩大逾一倍至0.5个百分点。穆迪分析首席经济学家Mark Zandi的判断明显更为悲观——他直言美国经济"脆弱"而非"韧性"，并将经济彻底失控的概率估计在三分之一左右。

Mark Zandi的警告则最为直接："如果利率在当前水平或更高水平再持续一两个季度，AI可能成为经济中首先断裂的那一环。"他指出，持续的高利率将压制AI相关股价，财富效应的逆转将进一步打压消费，而融资成本上升将使维持当前AI建设速度所需资本的筹集愈加困难。目前，AI在很大程度上依靠其自身的动能与市场乐观情绪运行，但这一状态的持续时间存在高度不确定性。

items.text:
美国银行衍生品团队发出警告，当AI泡沫最终破裂时，市场将呈现与过去数月截然不同的走势——不是"股跌债跌"（即股票下跌、美债收益率上升），而是股票与收益率同步下行。


10月8日，英国《金融时报》披露OpenAI年化收入远低于市场流传数字，当日纳斯达克指数重挫逾1%，费城半导体指数跌3.4%，而美债收益率也随即走低——债券市场表现出罕见的避险属性。美国银行衍生品团队在最新一期《全球股票波动率洞察》报告中将这次单日闪崩定性为"AI解仓的最佳预演"，并指出更关键的信号在于：彼时美债收益率与股市同步下行，而非出现市场几个月来已习以为常的"股跌债涨"格局。


这一模式随即在10月14日得到复制。当日美国CPI通胀数据超预期，10年期美债收益率一度飙升，加息预期概率短暂突破50%，但随着云计算基础设施企业CoreWeave股价崩跌逾15%、信用违约互换利差扩大135个基点，债市收益率涨势迅速逆转，收益率最终接近持平收盘。


15日，10年期美债收益率继续大幅下行10个基点至5.09%，触及三周低点。与此同时，MSCI亚太股票指数重挫逾3%，韩国综合指数单日一度暴跌9%，三星、SK海力士跌幅一度达到两位数。标普500期货跌0.4%，纳斯达克100期货跌逾1%。

美国银行认为，这正是AI泡沫破裂的"传导链条"：私人AI生态的压力最先、最猛烈地冲击纳斯达克，同时将债市拉向避险模式。


AI特有的风险冲击，纳斯达克首当其冲

美国银行股票挂钩团队Benjamin Bowler、Nitin Saksena、Arjun Goyal等人指出，10月8日纳斯达克对大盘的大幅跑输，与过去数年每一次AI特定风险事件的表现高度吻合——从2025年1月的DeepSeek冲击，到今年夏天的半导体板块回调，规律如出一辙。

报告认为，这反映了纳斯达克对"私人AI生态"的高敝口。OpenAI、Anthropic等私人AI公司一旦出现裂缝，纳斯达克100指数即为公开市场中首先承压的代理标的。该行将其定为AI交易——无论多空——的首选指数。


这一传导路径正面临新的压力测试。Anthropic于10月14日向华尔街开放财务数据，而OpenAI 200亿美元的"总收入与净收入缺口"仍悬而未决，私人端向公开市场的传导渠道料将持续受到考验。

债市异动：两次AI冲击均触发收益率同步下行

更值得关注的是债市的行为模式。过去数月，美股与美债收益率持续呈现反向关系，债券作为对冲工具的功能几乎失效。然而，10月8日与10月14日的两次AI风险事件均打破这一格局，收益率随股市同步走低。


美国银行将其归结为AI放缓的宏观逻辑：除传统避险资金流入外，AI投资周期降温意味着资本开支减少、电力及资源消耗下降，叠加对经济增长与通胀的双重压制，将对债券形成额外利好。换言之，若AI泡沫真正破裂，债券将重新发挥对冲功能。

报告援引的历史参照是2000年互联网泡沫破裂：彼时纳斯达克100指数崩盘，10年期美债收益率从约6.5%跌至4%中段。美国银行承认两个数据点尚不构成完整规律，但认为历史先例与宏观逻辑相互印证，已足以为投资者提供结构性参考。


CoreWeave引爆信用端危机，AI股本周跑输大盘840基点

10月14日的市场抛售揭示了AI泡沫另一潜在破裂路径：信用端。


CoreWeave（CRWV）是此次风暴中心。在其2032年到期债券G-spread突破1000个基点、收益率升至15%之后，股价随之崩跌逾15%，创上市以来第三大单日跌幅。D.A. Davidson分析师Gil Luria将CoreWeave定性为AI领域的"次级抵押贷款分级"，并警告若公司无法偿付债务，股价将归零——其融资成本约为9%，而投资回报率仅约1%。CoreWeave的信用违约互换利差当日扩大135个基点，市场目前隐含的五年内违约概率已达63%。

恐慌迅速蔓延。DigitalOcean（DOCN）下跌14%，Hut 8（HUT）跌10%，Nebius（NBIS）与IREN各跌约9%；Oracle（ORCL）下挫9%，与其信用违约互换点位的背离仍未弥合。市场研究机构Gartner随即发出警告，预计80%的新兴云计算企业将在2030年前停止独立运营。


本周，AI板块相对标普500非AI成分股的累计跑输幅度已达840个基点。BTIG策略师Jonathan Krinsky同样认为，当前的痛苦交易指向"利率下行、纳斯达克下行"，若"七巨头"也开始像半导体股那样随利率同步下跌，将进一步印证其"红色十月"判断。

美银推荐对冲组合：让债市补贴期权成本

面对这一潜在风险，美国银行衍生品团队提出了一套"以债补股"的对冲结构。


传统AI泡沫对冲的难点在于时机：过早买入看跌期权，市场持续走高将不断让行权价落后于市场。美国银行的解决方案是"最大回望看跌期权"（max lookback put）——其行权价随市场上涨而持续上移，但这一特性本身成本较高。该行的创新之处在于，将期权设定为在10年期SOFR低于当前远期利率25个基点时方才生效，以此将利率下行预期转化为期权费补贴。


具体交易方案为：买入纳斯达克100指数2027年9月到期、行权价为当前价格90%的每日观测最大回望看跌期权，附加利率触发条款，指示性期权费为3.62%，较纯回望看跌期权折价46%，亦低于普通看跌期权23个基点。


回测数据显示，对该结构进行过去30年的模拟定价，其触发概率为13%（普通90%看跌期权为11%），平均价内赔付倍数为7.2倍（普通看跌期权6.1倍，纯回望期权3.9倍），最大超额收益出现于互联网泡沫破裂期间。

该结构的主要风险在于2022年式的"股跌债涨"情景，即通胀冲击或美联储意外紧缩导致股债同向下跌的格局——这恰恰是2026年大部分时间债市的运行方式，并非真正的尾部风险。


此外，美国银行同步推荐一笔VIX看涨价差交易：买入VIX 11月到期19-24点价差，指示性成本0.63美元，最大赔付倍数约7.9倍，适用于对中期选举前后波动率温和抬升的判断。

泡沫程度几何：指标显示集中于局部而非全面

美国银行泡沫风险指标（BRI）的最新读数提供了更为细化的视角。标普500指数中目前仅有13只股票BRI超过0.8，合计占指数权重约2.4%；相比之下，互联网泡沫高峰期曾有50至100只股票触及该阈值，占指数权重20%至40%。

当前泡沫特征呈现出明显的集中性：单股层面，Moderna（MRNA）、CrowdStrike（CRWD）、惠普企业（HPE）、Zebra Technologies、Revvity及Palo Alto Networks（PANW）读数靠前；板块层面，美国银行旗下美国网络安全及巴西大选主题篮子BRI均达到0.92的高位。


值得注意的是，价格层面的泡沫指标显示风险仍属局部，但Jefferies已将当前局面定性为"AI的2008时刻"，并指出两家现金消耗型AI实验室合计占据2.3万亿美元订单积压的一半。这意味着真正的泡沫风险或并不体现在股价层面，而潜伏于资产负债表之中。

波动率被人为压制，一旦松动或触发急剧反弹

表面平静之下，市场结构已暗流涌动。标普500指数5日盘中已实现波动率仅为7.6%，处于过去一年的第三百分位。但美国银行认为，这种平静是被期权做市商手中庞大的gamma敞口人为维持的。


截至10月9日，标普500对冲型gamma读数为145亿美元，为过去一年第四高。大量0DTE/1DTE期权卖出流、衍生品收益基金的结构性波动率供给共同形成了市场的"防护栏"，将盘中波动控制在极窄区间。


然而，这一缓冲正在松动。据彭博宏观策略师Michael Ball指出，标普500已跌破7775至7750点的第一道支撑位；SpotGamma将"波动率触发点"定于7775点——低于此水平，做市商的对冲行为将不再起到平抑波动的作用。一旦指数跌破7700点附近，正向gamma将急剧稀薄，逢低买入的均值回归策略或将让位于"越跌越卖"模式。

与此同时，客户已悄然大量买入VIX看涨期权，仓位水平已接近2024年夏季高点——彼时曾引发剧烈波动。这一前瞻性波动率需求使标普500期限结构异常陡峭，1个月与1周平值隐含波动率之比处于过去一年的第95百分位。


美国银行估算，若前月VIX期货出现10点跳升，做市商为维持delta中性将被迫买入相当于约90%日均VIX期货成交量的头寸，为过去一年最高读数。高盛近期亦独立得出类似结论，认为VIX触及25点的概率高于标普500下跌2%的概率。两家银行不约而同地指向同一结论：一旦波动率松动，市场反应的烈度可能远超价格本身的跌幅。


后续关注节点：今日PPI数据、Anthropic财务披露，以及本月晚些时候的大型科技公司财报季，将对上述逻辑形成直接压力测试。若标普500无法收复7750点，做市商的gamma护盾将不复存在。

传统AI泡沫对冲的难点在于时机：过早买入看跌期权，市场持续走高将不断让行权价落后于市场。美国银行的解决方案是"最大回望看跌期权"（max lookback put）——其行权价随市场上涨而持续上移，但这一特性本身成本较高。该行的创新之处在于，将期权设定为在10年期SOFR低于当前远期利率25个基点时方才生效，以此将利率下行预期转化为期权费补贴。
具体交易方案为：买入纳斯达克100指数2027年9月到期、行权价为当前价格90%的每日观测最大回望看跌期权，附加利率触发条款，指示性期权费为3.62%，较纯回望看跌期权折价46%，亦低于普通看跌期权23个基点。
回测数据显示，对该结构进行过去30年的模拟定价，其触发概率为13%（普通90%看跌期权为11%），平均价内赔付倍数为7.2倍（普通看跌期权6.1倍，纯回望期权3.9倍），最大超额收益出现于互联网泡沫破裂期间。
该结构的主要风险在于2022年式的"股跌债涨"情景，即通胀冲击或美联储意外紧缩导致股债同向下跌的格局——这恰恰是2026年大部分时间债市的运行方式，并非真正的尾部风险。
此外，美国银行同步推荐一笔VIX看涨价差交易：买入VIX 11月到期19-24点价差，指示性成本0.63美元，最大赔付倍数约7.9倍，适用于对中期选举前后波动率温和抬升的判断。
泡沫程度几何：指标显示集中于局部而非全面
美国银行泡沫风险指标（BRI）的最新读数提供了更为细化的视角。标普500指数中目前仅有13只股票BRI超过0.8，合计占指数权重约2.4%；相比之下，互联网泡沫高峰期曾有50至100只股票触及该阈值，占指数权重20%至40%。
当前泡沫特征呈现出明显的集中性：单股层面，Moderna（MRNA）、CrowdStrike（CRWD）、惠普企业（HPE）、Zebra Technologies、Revvity及Palo Alto Networks（PANW）读数靠前；板块层面，美国银行旗下美国网络安全及巴西大选主题篮子BRI均达到0.92的高位。
值得注意的是，价格层面的泡沫指标显示风险仍属局部，但Jefferies已将当前局面定性为"AI的2008时刻"，并指出两家现金消耗型AI实验室合计占据2.3万亿美元订单积压的一半。这意味着真正的泡沫风险或并不体现在股价层面，而潜伏于资产负债表之中。
波动率被人为压制，一旦松动或触发急剧反弹
表面平静之下，市场结构已暗流涌动。标普500指数5日盘中已实现波动率仅为7.6%，处于过去一年的第三百分位。但美国银行认为，这种平静是被期权做市商手中庞大的gamma敞口人为维持的。

然而，这一缓冲正在松动。据彭博宏观策略师Michael Ball指出，标普500已跌破7775至7750点的第一道支撑位；SpotGamma将"波动率触发点"定于7775点——低于此水平，做市商的对冲行为将不再起到平抑波动的作用。一旦指数跌破7700点附近，正向gamma将急剧稀薄，逢低买入的均值回归策略或将让位于"越跌越卖"模式。

items.text:
AI叙事接连遭受冲击，正在以反直觉的逻辑重塑市场定价框架。在通胀数据火热出炉的背景下，美债收益率非但未见上行，反而随科技股暴跌一同俯冲。


10年期美债收益率周四在亚洲交易时段下行10个基点至5.09%，触及三周低点。与此同时，MSCI亚太股票指数重挫逾3%，韩国综合指数单日暴跌9%，三星电子与SK Hynix均重挫11%。标普500期货跌0.4%，纳斯达克100期货跌逾1%。避险资金大举涌入主权债市场，美元走软，黄金则在连续三日下跌后企稳回升至约4140美元/盎司。

此轮动荡并非通胀数据的单一驱动，云计算公司CoreWeave引发的AI产业链信用裂缝正快速传导至权益市场。CoreWeave股价周三暴跌逾17%，其2032年到期美元债收益率飙升至15%以上，五年期CDS走阔135个基点，市场隐含5年期违约概率已达63%。据彭博报道，多位分析师和投资人正重新评估AI板块整体融资风险敞口。

AI信用裂缝：CoreWeave成引爆点

CoreWeave的债务危机标志着本轮AI科技股杀跌从估值层面向信用层面的升级。该公司2032年到期高收益债在四个月前以面值发行，如今已跌至78美分以下，息差突破1000个基点。


D.A. Davidson分析师Gil Luria将CoreWeave定性为"AI领域的次贷资产"，警告其综合借贷成本约为9%，而资产投资回报率仅在1%左右，若无法维持债务周转，股权价值存在归零风险。


"美国CPI数据超预期与CoreWeave债券抛售，正促使投资者重新评估整个AI行业的融资风险，"Fibonacci Asset Management Global首席执行官Jung In Yun表示。


AI模型公司Anthropic的最新数据也令市场情绪承压。


据彭博援引知情人士称，该公司第三季度营收达168亿美元，但部分分析师认为该数字低于预期。“市场对Anthropic亮眼数据的失望，折射出对维持这一增长所需资本消耗的深层忧虑，"Vantage Global Prime高级市场分析师Hebe Chen表示，"在流动性已相当紧张的市场环境下，即将到来的IPO将进一步加剧这一担忧。"

"逆向逻辑"：AI退潮或推低美债收益率

通胀超预期本应推高美债收益率，但周三的市场走势打破了这一常规逻辑。


数据显示，美国9月CPI同比涨幅创五个月新高，核心通胀亦超预期，交易员一度将10月加息概率推升至50%以上。然而，长端美债收益率在短暂冲高后迅速回吐全部涨幅，几乎平收。

美国银行股票衍生品主管Benjamin Bowler团队在报告中指出，这已不是偶然，而是一种模式——本月内已出现两次相同形态：10月8日，媒体爆出OpenAI年化营收指引较市场预期低约200亿美元，当日纳指下跌的同时，美债收益率同样从早盘高点一路回落。


美银的分析认为，一旦市场开始计价AI放缓风险，资产相关性将发生彻底逆转。彭博Markets Live策略师Mark Cranfield亦指出，"此次风险可能与7月底的局面有所不同——AI泡沫破裂的风险有损经济增长，这次债券避险买盘或许持续更长时间。"


其背后的宏观逻辑直接而清晰：若AI资本支出放缓，算力建设的急刹车将重创供应链，同时压低市场对电力、大宗商品和高端硬件的需求预期——这不仅是对高估值的清算，更是对增长预期和通胀溢价的打击，最终反而利好债券。这一逻辑与2000年互联网泡沫破裂期间的宏观图景高度相似，彼时纳指崩溃过程中，10年期美债收益率自6.5%高位一路跌入4%区间。

尾部风险积聚：低波动下暗流涌动


表面数据上，美股波动率仍处于极低水平——标普500指数5日已实现波动率仅7.6%，处于过去一年前3%的低分位。但美银提示，这种平静在很大程度上由持有巨量Gamma头寸的做市商托底支撑，这层保护垫已出现松动迹象。


宏观策略师Michael Ball指出，标普500已击穿7775至7750的首道关键支撑。SpotGamma数据显示，做市商压制波动的"波动率触发位"恰在7775附近；若指数跌破7700，正向Gamma垫将快速消减，逢低买入和均值回归策略将全面失效，市场存在切入负反馈下行通道的风险。

与此同时，在现货波动率被大量期权收益型基金持续做空压制之际，买方机构正在大举买入VIX看涨期权，多头敞口已逼近2024年8月套利交易解除引发"闪崩"前夕的峰值水平。

items.text:
台积电公布强劲季度业绩，营收与利润均显著超越市场预期，公司连续第六个季度创下盈利纪录，印证全球人工智能芯片需求持续高涨。

公司周三公布，净利润达7631亿元新台币（约合236亿美元），同比增长68.7%，超出分析师平均预期的7395亿元新台币。同期营收达1.49万亿元新台币（约合467亿美元），同比增长50.9%，亦高于市场预期。该公司将毛利率指引下调至66.4%，略低于预期的66.5%，主要受2纳米制程初期量产拉低毛利的影响。

这份超预期业绩发布之际，市场对AI资本支出回报及长期融资可持续性的担忧正在升温。英伟达大客户、云服务提供商CoreWeave Inc.本周三股债双杀，大幅下挫。台积电的强劲表现为产业链上游提供了截然不同的信号，表明AI芯片需求目前仍维持强劲态势。

items.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
items.summary: A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's
items.text:
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".

As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.

But, here's we do know so far.

The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).

Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.

Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".

The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.

Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.

Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.

But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.

On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.

A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.

The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.

When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.

In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".

It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.

Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

items.text:
Warning: This story includes distressing content

A man has died after falling from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park on Monday in the US state of Georgia.

The man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was found dead under the ride after being ejected and hitting other people on it, according to police.

An investigation is under way and few details have yet to be released about what happened. Six Flags, the largest amusement park operator in North America, has temporarily closed nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.

Here's what we know so far about the incident.

The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.

"Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday.

"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction."

The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident.

The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review.

Officials have not held a news conference on the incident.

The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.

The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".

Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground.

"It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that."

He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him.

One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement.

Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed".

"Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen."

He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched.

Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood.

Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".

Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.

"I broke because we were just on there," she said.

Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer.

His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death.

He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach.

"Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account.

"His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did."

Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website.

The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.

According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool.

Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.

In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet.

In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.

With additional reporting by Brandon Drenon

items.text:
Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

[ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ]

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”

On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”

Divorcing safety from security

One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.

“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”

SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”

Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”

But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”

Bad cybersecurity could increase liability

If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions.

Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers.

However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok.

Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures.

BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.”

He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.”

SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”

What security leaders should do now

Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”

For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.”

But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”

“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”
